The case drew international attention and placed scrutiny on Goa’s tourism industry, which relies heavily on its reputation as a relaxed and safe destination. Critics alleged that police moved too quickly to classify the death as accidental, potentially overlooking evidence at the scene and delaying a proper homicide inquiry.

Goa Tourism Minister **Francisco X. Pacheco** was among those who publicly questioned the initial police response.

> “There has been a cover-up,” Pacheco said, calling for accountability and a deeper inquiry into whether police mishandled the investigation.

The allegations struck at a sensitive issue in Goa: the relationship between tourism, nightlife, drugs and law enforcement. Anjuna, where Keeling’s body was found, has long been associated with beach parties and a drug subculture that officials have struggled to control.

Police officials denied any deliberate attempt to suppress evidence or shield suspects.

Senior police officer **Kishan Kumar** defended the investigation, saying officers acted on the information available at the time.

But those assurances did little to quiet the controversy. MacKeown said the first police response was not merely flawed but dismissive, arguing that had she not challenged the initial findings, her daughter’s death may never have been treated as murder.

> “If I had accepted what I was first told, Scarlett’s case would have been closed as a drowning,” she said.
